title: Georgian Backs Physical AI and Quantum Tech in Canada
summary: Georgian's $5.8B venture fund invests in physical AI and quantum computing to anchor Canadian deep-tech firms at home. Defense, space, manufacturing surge.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Georgian Partners, managing $5.8 billion, now focuses on physical AI and quantum computing to keep Canadian startups from migrating south.
- Physical AI companies combining proprietary models, specialized hardware, and manufacturing operations are far harder to relocate than pure software firms.
- Defense and space sectors see renewed momentum under Prime Minister Carney's pro-business agenda, with firms like Dominion Dynamics and Kepler Communications scaling rapidly.


Georgian Partners, one of Canada's largest venture capital firms with $5.8 billion under management, is betting on physical artificial intelligence and[quantum computing](https://emergent.sh/glossary/quantum-computing) to reverse decades of brain drain. Co-founder Simon Chong sees the future inside a 95-year-old Campbell's Soup factory in Toronto, where Georgian-backed Xanadu Quantum Technologies plans to build quantum computer hardware. Officially launched on November 10, 2026, this strategic pivot targets companies whose physical assets make relocation nearly impossible.


## Why Physical AI Changes the Relocation Equation


Unlike pure software startups that can move headquarters overnight, physical AI companies embed artificial intelligence in machines, satellites, aircraft, and defense systems. These firms combine proprietary AI models, specialized hardware design, and established manufacturing operations. Once a company scales production facilities and supply chains, the cost of relocation becomes prohibitive.


Chong argues that Canada's battered manufacturing base, hit hard by US tariffs under President Donald Trump's trade war, now offers a strategic advantage. Decades of aerospace, automotive, and advanced materials production mean the country already has factories, supply chains, and skilled labor capable of building complex hardware. When a US venture capitalist demands relocation during a Series F round, founders can push back: the team, AI model development, hardware prototypes, and manufacturing infrastructure are already deeply rooted in Canada.


## Defense Renaissance Under Carney's Leadership


Prime Minister Mark Carney's pro-business agenda includes ramping up domestic defense procurement to meet NATO spending commitments. Georgian-backed Dominion Dynamics is developing Canada's first autonomous collaborative aircraft, an uncrewed physical AI plane designed to fly alongside piloted fighter jets in Arctic conditions. Founder Eliot Pence, a Canadian who built his career in the US before returning home, recently signed an agreement with Ukraine's Tencore to jointly manufacture uncrewed ground vehicles in Canada for the Ukrainian military.


Pence expects Dominion to become a major supplier in Carney's drone initiative, a co-production deal with Ukraine meant to bolster defenses against Russian aggression. However, scaling will require hundreds of millions in follow-on funding. Chong emphasizes that Georgian will take early-stage risk, but major institutional investors like Canadian pension funds and Brookfield Asset Management must step in for later rounds.


## Space Sector Sees Accelerated Growth


Canada has never launched a spacecraft into orbit from its own soil, but that may soon change. Ottawa leased a private spaceport in Nova Scotia, Carney signed a space cooperation pact with French President Emmanuel Macron, and Germany's Isar Aerospace is investing in Canadian launch infrastructure. Domestic launch companies including Canada Rocket Company, Reaction Dynamics, and NordSpace are expanding rapidly.


Kepler Communications, which builds satellites with onboard computing, received C$7 million from the federal government earlier in 2026 to advance engineering and commercialization. CEO Mina Mitry, who admitted that starting a deep-tech business in Canada a decade ago was a mistake, now says the environment has transformed beyond recognition in the past 12 months. Still, government funding must scale from millions to hundreds of millions to support companies like Dominion and Xanadu through growth stages.


## Trade Risks and Global Courtship


The ongoing stalemate in US-Canada trade talks raises questions about whether the country can attract long-term investment while tariff barriers remain. Chong is blunt: Canada cannot decouple from the US, which historically receives three-quarters of Canadian exports. Yet he sees new momentum, with Europe courting Canada as an associate member, global investors attending Carney's September investment summit in Toronto, and founders deliberately building companies that cannot be easily lifted out of the country.


Georgian's thesis depends on a fundamental shift: when founders raise large rounds from a position of strength, they can dictate terms, including where manufacturing and R&D operations stay. Chong sees this as a once-in-a-generation opportunity to fuse Canadian scientific talent with an established industrial base, keeping breakthrough innovations in quantum computing, autonomous systems, and satellite technology anchored at home.


## What This Means


Georgian's pivot to physical AI and quantum computing represents a calculated bet that hardware-intensive companies will resist the gravitational pull of Silicon Valley. If Carney's government can accelerate defense procurement, scale financial support, and attract institutional capital, Canada may finally retain the value it creates. The question is whether hundreds of millions in follow-on funding will materialize before competitors in the US and Europe outpace Canadian innovators.
